headline_en: Remittances still in Eid mood: USD 1.72 billion arrives in 19 days
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank data show expatriates sent USD 1,718.7 million in the first 19 days of April 2025, after a record USD 3.29 billion in March 2025. Bankers attribute the rise to reduced money laundering pushing senders to legal channels. Banks buy remittance dollars within the central bank ceiling of BDT 123, while the open market rate is about BDT 124.30.

facts.statement: Expatriates sent USD 171 crore 87 lakh (about USD 1.72 billion) to Bangladesh in the first 19 days of April 2025, more than USD 9 crore a day; the month was expected to reach around USD 300 crore if the trend continued.

Of remittances in the first 19 days of April 2025, state-owned banks brought USD 63 crore 97 lakh, the specialised Krishi Bank USD 9 crore, private banks about USD 99 crore and foreign banks USD 33 lakh 20 thousand.

Expatriates sent USD 329 crore to Bangladesh in March 2025, the highest for any single month ever; March 2024 was USD 199 crore, so growth was 64 percent. The first 24 days of March 2025 brought USD 270 crore through banking channels.
Remittances in February 2025 were USD 252 crore 80 lakh, 17 percent higher than a year earlier; January 2025 was 3 percent higher than January 2024.
For seven straight months after the August 2024 political change, expatriates sent more than USD 200 crore each month.

The article says that in 'the first eight months, July-March' of fiscal year 2024-25 expatriates sent USD 2,177 crore, about 28 percent more than USD 1,707 crore in the same period of 2023-24 (the article calls July-March eight months).
Banks in Bangladesh were buying remittance dollars within the central bank's ceiling of BDT 123 per dollar; in the open market the dollar was selling at up to BDT 124.30.
Bankers said expatriates are now choosing legal channels to send income mainly because money laundering has fallen; officials said the dollar shortage in banks has largely eased.

headline_en: A hospital owned by expatriates will be built: expatriates' welfare adviser
summary_en: Expatriates' welfare adviser Asif Nazrul said a hospital is planned on land near Baridhara, Dhaka, through a company in which expatriates would hold 40 to 50 percent of shares. He spoke at a Wage Earners' Welfare Board event on 16 April 2025 where 103 people received BDT 1.93 crore in grants, scholarships, insurance claims, compensation, medical aid and disability allowances. He also described the airport expatriate lounge facilities.

facts.statement: Adviser Asif Nazrul said the government wishes to build a hospital on land near Baridhara, Dhaka, through a company to be formed in which 40 to 50 percent of shares will be held by expatriates; only expatriates will be able to buy those shares. Expatriates would get treatment there and also be owners, with special discounts on treatment.
facts.source_in_article: Asif Nazrul, adviser, Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment

facts.statement: Asif Nazrul said not all returned workers can be given jobs in the planned hospital, but those returning from abroad with experience as nurses, cleaners, security guards and drivers will be tried for jobs on a priority basis.

Asif Nazrul said the expatriate lounge at the airport offers quality food at up to 30 percent lower prices, free Wi-Fi, free telephone, mobile charging and other facilities, and that airport staff have been given strict instructions to behave well with expatriates; he said harassment of expatriates at the airport has stopped because of steps taken.

At the Wage Earners' Welfare Board event on 16 April 2025 at Probashi Kalyan Bhaban auditorium, 12 families received BDT 36 lakh in financial grants (for workers who died abroad); 11 people received BDT 1 crore 4 lakh as insurance claims; two families received BDT 27 lakh 67 thousand as compensation, arrears and service benefits.

At the same 16 April 2025 event, 65 people received education scholarships, three people received BDT 3 lakh 30 thousand in medical assistance, and 10 people received BDT 1 lakh 20 thousand in disability allowance; in total 103 people received BDT 1 crore 93 lakh 13 thousand.

The Wage Earners' Welfare Board gives scholarships to children of expatriate families, disability allowance, medical assistance to sick expatriates, and financial grants, insurance and death compensation cheques to families of workers who die abroad.
It was said at the event that the assistance is not government money but expatriates' own money: the fee they deposit before going abroad is held in the Welfare Board's fund.

headline_en: Remittances close to USD 3 billion, a record before Eid
summary_en: Bangladesh received USD 294.5 crore in remittances in the first 26 days of March 2025, on course to pass USD 3 billion in a month for the first time. Bankers credit lower money laundering; banks buy remittance dollars within the BDT 123 ceiling.

facts.statement: Remittances to Bangladesh in the first 26 days of March 2025 were USD 294 crore 50 lakh, including USD 19 crore 70 lakh in the last two days; the daily average for the month was USD 11 crore 32 lakh.

March 2025 remittance flow: USD 166 crore in the first 15 days; USD 225 crore by 19 March (USD 13 crore on 19 March alone); USD 243 crore in the first 22 days; USD 270 crore by 24 March. The first week averaged USD 11 crore a day and the second week USD 12 crore a day.
Before Eid-ul-Fitr in 2024, USD 45 crore in remittances came in five days, an average of USD 9 crore a day. Remittances usually come in more before the two Eids than in any other month.

Remittances in February 2025 were USD 252 crore 80 lakh, 17 percent higher than a year earlier; January 2025 was 3 percent higher than January 2024; expatriates have sent over USD 200 crore a month for seven months since August 2024.
The article says that in 'the first eight months, July-March' of fiscal year 2024-25 expatriates sent USD 1,849 crore, 24 percent more than USD 1,493 crore in the same period of 2023-24.

Banks in Bangladesh were buying remittance dollars within the central bank ceiling of BDT 123; competition between banks to buy remittance dollars had fallen. Earlier the dollar had once risen to BDT 128.
Bankers said expatriates chose legal channels mainly because money laundering has fallen.

summary_en: Bangladesh received USD 225 crore in remittances through banks in the first 19 days of March 2025, a Ramadan record pace. From July 2024 to 19 March 2025 remittances reached USD 2,074 crore, 27 percent above a year earlier.

headline_en: How remittances are rising even though the dollar price is not
summary_en: The article explains how money-transfer aggregators bid up the dollar after 2022 and how the post-August 2024 rate cap (BDT 122 plus up to BDT 1) and monitoring calmed the market. The central bank governor said Saudi remittances are being routed via Dubai by a ring that hoards and resells them at higher prices. In the first 15 days of March 2025 USD 166 crore arrived, with banks paying BDT 122.80 to 123.

facts.statement: Remittances to Bangladesh used to come directly into the recipient's bank account, and recipients could also collect remittances from banks and various private organisations using a one-time password; the article says this can still be done.

When the dollar shortage began in 2022, some overseas money-transfer companies began buying remittance dollars from customers and from smaller similar firms, pooling them and bargaining with Bangladeshi banks; the bank offering the highest price got the dollars, which drove the dollar price up sharply.

After the new government formed in August 2024 the dollar price was fixed at BDT 122; later it was decided that banks could buy and sell dollars at up to BDT 1 more, and the central bank tightened monitoring of the rates banks use.

Bangladesh Bank governor Ahsan H. Mansur said at several events that not all remittances from Saudi Arabia now come directly to Bangladesh but come via Dubai: a dishonest ring buys remittances in Saudi Arabia, hoards them and sells them to Bangladeshi banks at a higher price, trying to destabilise Bangladesh's dollar market from there. He said banks would not be allowed to buy dollars at higher prices from such firms.
facts.source_in_article: Ahsan H. Mansur, governor, Bangladesh Bank

facts.statement: Former Bangladesh Bank chief economist Mustafa K. Mujeri said remittance-friendly policies should make sending easier; if remittance money arrived instantly through banking channels the illegal route would largely close; and people going abroad should be sent with somewhat more skills to raise flows.
facts.source_in_article: Mustafa K. Mujeri, former chief economist, Bangladesh Bank

facts.statement: In the first 15 days of March 2025 (Ramadan) USD 166 crore in remittances came through banks: USD 81 crore in the first week and USD 85 crore in the second. Daily averages were USD 11 crore and USD 12 crore.

In the first 15 days of March 2025 Islami Bank received the most remittances, about USD 30 crore; Janata Bank about USD 14 crore; Krishi Bank USD 13 crore; BRAC Bank USD 9 crore; Trust Bank USD 8 crore 97 lakh; City Bank USD 8 crore 95 lakh.

Banks said the buying price of a remittance dollar was within BDT 123; most banks bought above BDT 122.80 but none exceeded BDT 123. City Bank managing director Mashrur Arefin said his bank was buying at BDT 122.80 to 123.
facts.source_in_article: bank sources; Mashrur Arefin, MD, City Bank

facts.statement: Bank treasury officials said legal-channel remittances rose because money laundering has fallen and because there is no instability over the dollar price.

Expatriates sent USD 252 crore 80 lakh in February 2025; since the August 2024 political change they have sent on average over USD 200 crore a month for seven months; March 2025 could exceed USD 300 crore.
Before Eid-ul-Fitr in 2024, USD 45 crore in remittances came in 5 days (USD 9 crore a day).

headline_en: Western countries overtake the Middle East as top remittance sources
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank's January 2025 source-country data show the United States first and the United Kingdom second, together sending USD 68 crore (31 percent) of USD 219 crore. Bankers say this is largely a recording effect: large money-transfer firms such as Western Union and MoneyGram aggregate remittances from many countries and send them from the country where they are registered or headquartered.

facts.statement: In January 2025 Bangladesh received about USD 219 crore in remittances, of which USD 68 crore or 31 percent was recorded as coming from the United States and the United Kingdom.

Remittances recorded from the United States to Bangladesh were USD 56.5 crore in December 2024 and about USD 41 crore in January 2025, a fall of about USD 15 crore, yet the US remained the top source; it has been top since September 2024, having overtaken the UAE which was top in August 2024.

The United Kingdom rose from fifth place in December 2024 (about USD 25 crore) to second place in January 2025 (about USD 27.25 crore) among remittance sources for Bangladesh, a rise of USD 2.25 crore or over 9.25 percent.

In December 2024 the UAE was the second largest remittance source for Bangladesh with USD 37 crore; Saudi Arabia was third with USD 29 crore; Malaysia fourth (the article says 'in May about USD 26 crore came from Malaysia'); the UK fifth with about USD 25 crore. Remittances from the UAE, Malaysia and Saudi Arabia fell notably in January 2025 compared with December.
Total remittances to Bangladesh fell from USD 264 crore in December 2024 to USD 219 crore in January 2025.

In January 2025 the Middle East countries UAE, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Bahrain, Jordan, Iraq and Lebanon together sent USD 95 crore in remittances to Bangladesh, against USD 68 crore from the US and UK. Other large sources include Italy, France, Greece and Portugal.

Mutual Trust Bank managing director Syed Mahbubur Rahman said large remittance companies now collect income from all countries and then send it to the destination from one specific country, which is why remittances recorded from the US and UK suddenly rose. Bankers said Western Union, MoneyGram and others use an aggregated method, so remittances are recorded under the country where the company is registered or headquartered.

headline_en: Islami, Sonali, BRAC, Trust and Agrani banks are top five for remittances
summary_en: Five banks handled about USD 92 crore of the USD 218.52 crore in remittances Bangladesh received in January 2025. Islami Bank stayed first with USD 28.22 crore; bankers say its presence in labour-destination countries is larger than any other bank's.

facts.statement: In January 2025 Islami Bank, Sonali Bank, BRAC Bank, Trust Bank and Agrani Bank together brought about USD 92 crore of Bangladesh's USD 218 crore 52 lakh in remittances; the article gives the share both as 'about half or 45 percent' and as 42 percent.
Remittances through Islami Bank were USD 28 crore 22 lakh in January 2025 (about USD 37 crore in December 2024), keeping it first among Bangladeshi banks.

Remittances through Sonali Bank were about USD 18 crore in January 2025 (USD 21 crore in December), second; BRAC Bank USD 16 crore 27 lakh (USD 19 crore 32 lakh in December), third; Trust Bank USD 16 crore 15 lakh (USD 18 crore 44 lakh in December), fourth; Agrani Bank USD 13.5 crore (USD 26 crore 48 lakh in December, when it was second), fifth.

People in the banking sector said Islami Bank's presence in the Middle East and other countries with many Bangladeshi workers is greater than any other bank's, which is why it gets the largest response from expatriates sending money home.
Total remittances were USD 218 crore 52 lakh in January 2025 against USD 264 crore in December 2024, a fall of USD 45.5 crore or 17.25 percent.

summary_en: Expatriates sent USD 218.52 crore to Bangladesh through banks in January 2025, 3.4 percent more than January 2024. The seven-month fiscal-year total was USD 1,596.18 crore, USD 305 crore more than a year earlier.

Of January 2025 remittances, state-owned banks brought USD 51 crore 11 lakh, specialised banks USD 11 crore 60 lakh, private banks USD 155 crore 15 lakh, and foreign banks 'USD 65 crore' as printed (the four figures as printed add up to more than the stated monthly total).

headline_en: United States now tops the list of remittance-sending countries
summary_en: Bangladesh Bank's September-November 2024 report shows the United States as the top recorded remittance source for three straight months, with about USD 140 crore against the UAE's USD 99 crore. Bank executives say global remittance firms buy remittances from small firms in many countries and send them from one country, so the US is recorded as the source.

facts.statement: About USD 140 crore in remittances to Bangladesh was recorded from the United States in September-November 2024, the top source for three straight months; the UAE was second with USD 99 crore. Next in the top ten were Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, the United Kingdom, Kuwait, Italy, Oman, Qatar and Singapore, in that order.

Remittances recorded from the United States to Bangladesh: August 2024 USD 29 crore 34 lakh; September about USD 39 crore (over 34 percent growth); October USD 50 crore (over 28 percent growth); November USD 51 crore 19 lakh.
Remittances from the UAE to Bangladesh: August 2024 USD 34 crore (then the top source, USD 5 crore more than the US); September USD 36 crore; October USD 33 crore; November USD 29 crore.

Top executives of several banks said large global remittance companies now buy remittances from small firms in various countries, pool them and send them to the destination country from one specific country; Western Union, MoneyGram and others use this aggregated method, sending from the United States, so the US is recorded as the source country.

headline_en: Reserves up, overdue import liabilities down
summary_en: Bangladesh received a record USD 263.9 crore in remittances in December 2024, and about USD 2,700 crore in calendar 2024, 23 percent above 2023. Gross reserves rose to about USD 2,650 crore and banks cleared about USD 330 crore of overdue foreign liabilities in five months. Officials credit reduced money laundering and hundi and banks paying more for remittance dollars.

facts.statement: Expatriates sent USD 263 crore 90 lakh to Bangladesh in December 2024, the highest monthly remittance in the country's history; the previous record was USD 259 crore in July 2020. December 2023 was USD 199 crore 10 lakh, so growth was 32.54 percent.

In all of 2024 remittances to Bangladesh were about USD 2,700 crore, 23 percent more than in 2023. July-December 2024 was USD 1,377 crore against USD 1,080 crore in July-December 2023, growth of 26.75 percent.
Remittances: August 2024 USD 222 crore; September USD 240 crore; October USD 239 crore (21 percent above a year earlier); November USD 220 crore (about 14 percent above USD 193 crore).

Bank officials said Bangladesh Bank had instructed banks to clear old import liabilities within December 2024, so many banks bought remittance dollars at higher prices and expatriates sent more through banking channels.

Mutual Trust Bank MD Syed Mahbubur Rahman said that after the change of government indiscriminate bank lending fell, so money laundering fell and hundi came under control. Bangladesh Bank spokesperson Husne Ara Shikha said expatriates came forward after the July-August mass movement, hundi was somewhat controlled because laundering fell, and banks focused more on collecting remittances to settle overdue foreign liabilities.

headline_en: Government giving scholarships to children of expatriate workers
summary_en: The Wage Earners' Welfare Board is giving scholarships to meritorious children of expatriate workers who passed SSC in 2024 or HSC in 2023. The article gives the GPA thresholds, duration, eligibility, required documents, the online application sites and the 25 November to 24 December (2024) application window.

facts.statement: The government's Wage Earners' Welfare Board gives scholarships to meritorious children of expatriate workers. Eligible to apply: children who passed SSC or equivalent in 2024 and enrolled in class eleven or equivalent or a diploma course in Bangladesh, or who passed HSC or equivalent in 2023 and are studying at a university or medical college in Bangladesh.

Results required for the Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship: SSC or equivalent GPA 5.00 in science and GPA 4.75 in humanities and commerce; HSC or equivalent GPA 4.80 in science and GPA 4.50 in humanities and commerce. Children of workers who died abroad need only GPA 4.00 from any group.

Duration of the Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship: secondary-category recipients are covered for the next two years (those in higher secondary) and diploma students for four years; in the higher-secondary category, undergraduate students get 3 to 4 years and medical students 5 years.

Children of expatriates who are members of the Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Training (BMET) or the Wage Earners' Welfare Board can apply for the scholarship; children of deceased expatriate workers who have received or will receive a financial grant from the Board are also considered.

The Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship application is online only. The application must give the student's and guardian's mobile numbers, and include proof that the mother or father is an expatriate worker, the student's photo and signature, a copy of birth registration or national ID, and a certificate from the current educational institution.

A scholarship application to the Wage Earners' Welfare Board is cancelled if the mother's or father's name on the student's certificate does not match the expatriate worker's passport, or if there is any other error.
Online scholarship applications to the Wage Earners' Welfare Board go through www.wewb.gov.bd or stipen.wewb.gov.bd/stipend (as printed).
The application window for the Wage Earners' Welfare Board scholarship (2024 round) was 25 November to 24 December.

Remittances from the UAE to Bangladesh were USD 33, 34, 36 and 33 crore in July, August, September and October 2024 respectively; the UAE was the top source in August 2024 and fell to second in September and October.

In October 2024 Bangladesh received about USD 240 crore in remittances, of which about 21 percent came from the US and 13.75 percent from the UAE; the two together sent USD 83 crore, 35 percent of the total.

Mutual Trust Bank MD Syed Mahbubur Rahman said Western Union, MoneyGram and other remittance companies now collect remittances from various countries and send them to the destination from one place, so higher US figures may not mean actual remittances from the US rose; income from other countries passes through large firms and arrives from the US, making the growth appear on paper.

headline_en: Canada's new work permit rules for students take effect in November
summary_en: Canada's immigration department IRCC announced revised Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) rules effective 1 November 2024. University degree graduates stay eligible for up to three years regardless of field, but college graduates must have studied one of 966 listed programmes in five fields, and all applicants must meet language scores (CLB 7 for university, CLB 5 for college). Tourism, hospitality and business studies are not on the list.

facts.statement: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) announced revised Post-Graduation Work Permit (PGWP) rules effective 1 November 2024. Students who applied for or received a study permit before 1 November 2024 remain eligible under the existing rules; those who apply on or after that date fall under the new rules.
IRCC confirmed that university degree graduates remain eligible for a Post-Graduation Work Permit of up to three years with no restriction based on field of study.

From 1 November 2024, graduates of college programmes in Canada must have completed study in a designated field to qualify for a PGWP. IRCC listed 966 eligible programmes covering five fields: agriculture and agri-food; healthcare; science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM); skilled trades; and transportation.
Fields traditionally popular with foreign students such as tourism, hospitality and business studies are not on Canada's list of PGWP-eligible college programmes.

PGWP applicants must prove English or French ability through an approved language test: university graduates need Canadian Language Benchmarks (CLB) 7 in English or the French equivalent NCLC 7; college graduates need CLB 5 or NCLC 5 in all four skills (reading, writing, listening, speaking).

A Toronto Star report said more than 105,000 students were given Post-Graduation Work Permits in the first half of 2024; 64 percent were college programme graduates; business studies graduates were 42 percent and all STEM fields 37 percent.

Karen Dancey, director of recruitment and international at Olds College, said on LinkedIn that hospitality's absence from the list would be disastrous for rural and remote communities. According to ICEF Monitor, Colleges Ontario president and CEO Marketa Evans raised the same concern in an open letter to IRCC minister Marc Miller in September, criticising lack of consultation with provinces (the article attributes the letter's quoted words to Marc Miller).

summary_en: Bangladesh received USD 153 crore in remittances (about BDT 18,360 crore) in the first 19 days of October 2024. Islami Bank brought the most. Bankers say many expatriates now respond to campaigns to send money legally, reversing the July-August campaign against legal channels.

facts.statement: Bangladesh received USD 153 crore in remittances in the first 19 days of October 2024, about BDT 18,360 crore: government banks USD 40 crore, specialised banks USD 7 crore 81 lakh, private banks USD 105 crore.

September 2024 remittances were USD 240 crore, the second highest of 2024; the highest was USD 254 crore in June 2024, a three-year record; USD 259 crore came in July 2020.

Governor Ahsan H. Mansur (in office from 14 August 2024) widened the interbank foreign-exchange band from 1 percent to 2.5 percent, letting banks raise the crawling-peg mid-rate from BDT 117 to a maximum of BDT 120, so banks could pay somewhat more for remittances.

During the July-August 2024 student-public movement there was a campaign not to send remittances through legal channels; bankers said that has changed and many now respond to campaigns to send remittances legally through banking channels.

headline_en: Italy taking back 12 Bangladeshi and Egyptian migrants from Albania
summary_en: Twelve Bangladeshi and Egyptian migrants whom Italy had sent to an asylum camp in Albania under a five-year Italy-Albania agreement left for Italy on 19 October 2024 after Italian judges ruled against the transfers. Sixteen had been sent on 16 October, four of whom were returned at once as vulnerable. Italy's interior minister said he would appeal.

facts.statement: Under a five-year Italy-Albania agreement signed in November 2023, male migrants arriving in Italy are to be sent first to Albania and held in an Albanian asylum camp until Italian courts finish examining their immigration cases.

On Wednesday 16 October 2024, 16 Bangladeshi and Egyptian migrants reached Albania's Shengjin port from Italy, the first group sent under the Italy-Albania agreement; four were immediately returned to Italy because their condition was 'vulnerable'.
On Saturday 19 October 2024 the remaining 12 Bangladeshi and Egyptian migrants left Albania on an Italian coast guard vessel to be taken to Brindisi in southern Italy.

On Friday 18 October 2024 Italian judges ruled against the Italy-Albania transfers, saying a recent European Court of Justice ruling means the male migrants sent to Albania must be brought back to Italy. Interior minister Matteo Piantedosi announced an appeal to a higher Italian court, and prime minister Giorgia Meloni said on social media she would do everything to stop illegal immigration.
